title: Detection Strategy for Masquerading via Legitimate Resource Name or Location
shortTitle: Detection Strategy for Masquerading via Legitimate Resour...
summary: This detection strategy covers Masquerading by matching a legitimate resource name or location (T1036.005), where an adversary names a payload after a trusted system or vendor component, or drops it into a directory that users and tools already trust. The technique matters because analysts, allowlists and application control policies often key on file names and paths, so a trusted looking name can buy the attacker execution and time. Detection depends on process creation telemetry that carries the full image path, the original file name from the version resource, the signing state, and on file creation records inside system or program directories. It fails most often because legitimate third party software also places binaries in trusted looking paths.

beginner.definition: This detection looks for a program that uses a trusted name or a trusted folder. An attacker may name a harmful program after a normal Windows part. They may also put it in a folder where you expect only system files.
beginner.whyItMatters: People trust names and folders. If a program is called the same as a Windows component, many tools will allow it. A quick look at the file name will not raise any doubt. This trick also helps an attacker hide among the many system processes that run all day. To catch it, you must check the full path and the file signature, not only the name.
howItWorks: The system logs every new process together with the full path of the program that started it.
The rule keeps the process names that belong to the operating system or to a trusted vendor.
It then checks the folder, because those names should come from one expected location.
A match from a temporary, downloads or user folder is treated as suspicious.
The rule also reads the original file name inside the program and the signature on it.
When the name, the folder and the signature do not agree, an alert is raised.
beginner.example: Think of a building where the cleaners wear a uniform and carry a pass. A stranger can buy a similar uniform and walk past the desk. The uniform alone convinces nobody who checks the pass. The file path and the signature are your pass check.
takeaways: Judge a program by its path, its signature and its name together.
A system process name outside the system folder is a strong signal.
Allowlists based only on file names will let masquerading through.

objectives: Explain how trusted file names and trusted folders are used to avoid scrutiny
Identify process and file telemetry fields that reveal a mismatch between name, path and publisher
Establish the expected install locations for system binaries and approved applications
Write a rule that combines image path, original file name and signature state instead of the name alone
Triage a match by hashing the file and checking it against known good software inventory
Describe the coverage gap when application control already blocks user writable directories
dataSources: Sysmon event 1 process creation with image path, original file name, signature and signature status
Windows Security event 4688 process creation with command line auditing enabled
Sysmon event 11 file creation of new executables inside system, program and vendor directories
Sysmon event 7 image load records showing unsigned modules loaded into a trusted process
Software inventory and endpoint file metadata providing the expected publisher and hash for installed programs
logic: The pattern is a process whose file name matches a trusted system or vendor component but whose full image path, original file name or signature does not match that component. The fields that must be correlated are the image path, the file name, the original file name from the version resource, the signing status and publisher, the parent process and the user. The benign case is a signed third party component that carries a vendor name such as a service host and installs under its own program directory, or an operating system binary invoked from a compatibility path. The malicious case is a system sounding executable running from a user writable directory, with no valid signature or with a publisher that does not match the claimed product, often created minutes before it ran.
pseudoQuery:
# title: System Process Name Running From User Writable Path
# logsource:
#   product: windows
# detection:
#   selection_name:
#     Image|endswith:
#       - '\\svchost.exe'
#       - '\\lsass.exe'
#       - '\\services.exe'
#   filter_expected_path:
#     Image|startswith: 'C:\\Windows\\System32\\'
#   condition: selection_name and not filter_expected_path
# level: high
falsePositives: Third party backup or security agents that ship a helper binary with a name that resembles an operating system component
Software development kits that copy a system named utility into a project build folder for testing
End user support tools that place a signed diagnostic binary into a user profile directory
Application compatibility shims that launch a system binary from a redirected virtualisation path
tuningNotes: Build the rule from the real install paths you observe for each trusted name, and filter signed binaries whose publisher matches the expected product, which removes most third party agent noise. Keep the temporary, downloads and public folders unfiltered, because that is where the value of the rule lies. Add the original file name comparison so that renaming a payload to a trusted name still triggers when the internal metadata does not agree. Narrowing by signature reduces false positives but misses a masquerading binary that carries a stolen valid signature, so track new signers over time and review them monthly.
